seo.title: Karmic tail 6 17 11 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 17 11 compatibility: what The Lovers, The Star and Strength mean in a couple's destiny matrix, and why its story is Cupid and Psyche.

title: Karmic tail 6-17-11 in compatibility: The Lovers, The Star and Strength
short: The 6-17-11 tail sounds like a wedding toast: love, a star, strength. In a couple's destiny matrix, though, it is not a wish but a task, and its story is ancient — Apuleius's tale of Cupid and Psyche. The couple enters the task through the wish for love (6, The Lovers), lives it out in a light that shows everything that was hidden (17, The Star), and has one main thing to learn: to handle the force of their own feelings so that the union holds neither a beast nor a tamer (11, Strength).

sections.h2: The tale told to a bride
paragraphs: In the second century Apuleius set into his novel the Metamorphoses, better known as The Golden Ass, a tale that outlived both the novel and the empire. It is told by a drunken old woman in a robbers' cave to a girl who has been kidnapped straight from her wedding. "But I will take your mind off it at once with pretty stories and old wives' tales," she says (here and below, Apuleius is quoted in our own translation from the Latin). A bride whose wedding was stolen is told about a wedding that looks like a funeral.

A king has three daughters, and the youngest, Psyche, is so beautiful that people forget the way to the temples of Venus. The offended goddess sends her son, Cupid, to make the girl fall for the lowest of mortals. And the oracle of Apollo orders her father:

"King, on a crag of a high mountain set the girl / adorned for a funeral wedding; / hope for no son-in-law of mortal stock, / but a cruel, wild, viperish evil. / … / Jupiter himself trembles before it, and the gods are afraid."

The wedding torches blacken with soot, the flute slips into a mournful key, and "tearful Psyche goes not to her wedding but to her own funeral." From the cliff the west wind, Zephyr, carries her off to a palace where invisible servants wait on her and where, at night, a husband comes whom she must never see. Her sisters visit, see the gold and grow envious. They convince Psyche that a huge serpent sleeps with her at night and teach her to hide a razor in the bed and a lamp under a pot. At night Psyche raises the lamp and sees "the gentlest and sweetest of all wild beasts — that very Cupid himself." A drop of hot oil falls on the god's shoulder; he wakes and flies away.

Then come wanderings and four impossible tasks set by Venus. The last of them is a descent to the underworld for a box of beauty, which Psyche opens on the way back, and she falls into a deathlike sleep. Cupid wakes her with a prick of his arrow. Jupiter summons the gods, promises that the marriage "will not be unequal" and hands Psyche a cup of ambrosia — the mortal becomes immortal. The couple have a daughter, "whom we call Pleasure."

The three cards of the 6-17-11 tail are three acts of this tale. The Lovers are the night palace, where one loves without seeing a face. The Star is the lamp in whose light everything shows. Strength is the beast of the oracle, the one everyone feared, who turned out to be love. And at the centre of the chart, for 98.8% of these couples, stands 13, Death — that very wedding in funeral dress. The tale promises the couple neither monsters nor trials set by a goddess. Its use is different: in it one recognises the order in which the three forces stand in the tail, and what happens between them.

sections.h2: Waite's clues: Cupid, the butterfly and the mystery of union
paragraphs: Linking the tale to the tail is our reading, but it rests on more than the plot: the clues are in the writing of Waite, the author of the classic deck. The pictures he discusses come from old decks and from the Waite–Smith deck; the cards on this site do not show these details, but Waite's words concern the meaning of the cards themselves.

The first clue is in The Lovers. Describing an old eighteenth-century card on which father, mother and child stand beneath a flying Cupid, Waite calls the pagan god a misapplied emblem of marriage and explains why: "The Cupid is of love beginning rather than of love in its fulness, guarding the fruit thereof." The formula of the tail's first point is written almost word for word. The couple's entry to the task is Cupid, love that is only beginning. The task is to reach fullness.

The second is in The Star. In his historical notes Waite remarks in passing: "A bird is perched on a tree near her; for this a butterfly on a rose has been substituted in some later cards." In Greek, ψυχή, psyche, means soul, and Aristotle uses the same word for a butterfly. Artists have often given Psyche butterfly wings. In the middle of the tail stands a card on which Psyche once settled.

The third is in Strength. Waite writes that "Fortitude, in one of its most exalted aspects, is connected with the Divine Mystery of Union", and that "there is one aspect in which the lion signifies the passions." The couple's main task stands on the card of union, and its beast is not an enemy outside but passion. That is exactly what Apuleius told: the viperish evil of the oracle, before which Jupiter trembles, is the god of love.

The fourth is in Death, the card of the centre. Waite's divinatory list contains a line that seems copied from Psyche's wedding: "for a maid, failure of marriage projects." And his description of the symbol holds the way the tale ends: "The veil or mask of life is perpetuated in change, transformation and passage from lower to higher."

sections.h2: Entry to the task: The Lovers, or loving without seeing a face
paragraphs: The first point of a couple's tail is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a common language. The task begins with this wish. But the point stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also turn into resistance.

In the 6-17-11 tail the wish is love itself. Not so much a home, a project or a joint venture as a state: to be in love, to choose and be chosen, to live as if it were still the beginning. Waite calls The Lovers "the card of human love". Wen sees in them "a strong feeling of paradise, at least in the beginning", and warns that "the feeling of paradise may be evanescent if caution is not observed."

Apuleius has a sentence that names this entry better than any other. Studying her sleeping husband's weapons by lamplight, Psyche tests the point of one of his arrows and pricks her finger until it bleeds. "So, without knowing it, Psyche of her own accord fell in love with Love." To fall in love with Love is a wonderful start and an honest wish. It becomes resistance when love of love crowds out interest in the person.

Even before the lamp, Psyche tells her invisible husband: "Whoever you are, I love you desperately, as my own soul, and I would not compare you even with Cupid himself." The irony is that there is no one to compare him with: he is Cupid. But the key words are "whoever you are". It is easy to love without knowing who is beside you: wishes fill in the portrait.

This is exactly where the sisters catch her out. The first time, she describes her husband as a young man "whose cheeks are just shaded with down", a hunter. The second time, as a middle-aged merchant "with a sprinkling of grey". "Either the wretch made it all up, or she has never set eyes on her husband," the sisters conclude. For a couple this is a familiar scene: to a friend the partner is described one way, to the parents another, to oneself a third, and all three portraits are sincere. This is not a lie. It is a person no one has yet seen in the light.

In Lisovskaya, The Lovers among a couple's tasks are recognised by scenes: the relationship is measured against an ideal and always comes up short; insecurity rereads someone else's messages at night; no decision is taken without a family council. In the tale all of this fits into two words: in tears, Psyche calls her palace "a blissful prison". The wish to keep the enchantment quietly grows prohibitions — don't ask, don't look, don't talk about hard things, so as not to scare it away. Cupid sets his wife exactly this condition. For a couple it is more often a silent agreement that nobody ever announced out loud.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: The Star, the lamp and the drop of oil
paragraphs: Lisovskaya does not interpret the middle of a couple's tail separately: it is an "addition" to the main point. On this site it is read as the path — what the couple does and goes through on the way from the wish to the main task. This is the product's reading, not a statement from the book.

For this couple the path is lit by The Star, the card of open truth: Waite connects it with "Truth unveiled". For two people these are the moments when the partner is suddenly seen whole: the first honest talk about money or fears, a weakness seen without the scenery, a dream said out loud for the first time. Of The Star at its best, Lisovskaya writes that such partners often understand who they want to be only as a couple, and tell each other plainly what they like and what they don't. This is the case where the pretty picture of a union turns out to be true.

Psyche's lamp shows exactly this. She went to kill a serpent and saw the one she had loved blindly. In the light, this couple is more likely to discover the best than the worst — that is hope, The Star's second name.

But light here is never free. Psyche's hand trembles, and the lamp — "or because it, too, longed to touch and, as it were, to kiss so fair a body" — spits oil on the god's shoulder. Apuleius cannot help himself and turns to address it: "Oh bold and reckless lamp, worthless servant of love, you burn the very god of all fire!" Truth seen in secret burns. Waite's list of meanings for The Star, by the way, begins not with hope but with "loss" and "abandonment" — what Psyche receives a minute after the light.

The Star among a couple's tasks has a reverse side, and the tale knows it too. Psyche shows her sisters around the palace and loads them with gold — she puts her happiness on display, and displayed happiness breeds envy. In the book's worked example where The Star falls among a couple's tasks, Lisovskaya notes that such a couple's tasks may play out in public. The Star's downside shows in scenes: the couple's photos are better than its evenings; the partner is compared with other people's husbands and wives; one is quietly fitted to an image that is convenient to show; one's own dream is shelved, and the other's dream is obstructed along the way.

The most precise scene is Proserpina's box. Psyche opens it to take a little of the divine beauty and "so please that beautiful lover of mine", but there is "nothing there at all, no beauty whatever, only an infernal sleep, a truly Stygian one." Beauty fetched for the picture turns out to be an empty box.

sections.h2: Main task: Strength and the beast of the oracle
paragraphs: The main point of a couple's tail is its main task, its chief difficulties and trials. Lisovskaya reads this point mostly through its downside: what the couple is not managing and what it has to learn.

The oracle promised Psyche a monster, "a cruel, wild, viperish evil", before which Jupiter himself trembles. It is a portrait of Cupid: winged, armed with fire and arrows, stronger than the gods. The beast feared in this tale is love, or rather its force: passion, jealousy, the power of one person over another. Strength as the main task tells the couple the same thing: the main trial is not an outside enemy but the energy that lives between two people.

Wen writes that "the Strength card is about domination over the Seeker's fears" and reminds that "the Seeker cannot use brute force to exercise will over others; the Seeker must use gentle, subtle influence." In Lisovskaya, Strength at its worst is an argument over who is in charge at home that drags on for years; each has their own truth, and both are loud; a jibe in front of guests, after which the other says nothing until evening. And the task is respect: to share the housework fairly, to balance work and family, and from the very start to say what one likes and what one doesn't.

In Apuleius's tale there is not a single equal agreement. Cupid sets the condition: don't look and don't ask. Psyche answers with a razor hidden in the bed. Venus declares her daughter-in-law a runaway servant, and one of her household shouts at Psyche: "So, most worthless of maids, have you at last learned that you have a mistress?" The sisters advise murder. And in Aksakov's The Scarlet Flower (Alenky tsvetochek), a Russian relative of this tale, power is turned the other way round: the forest monster writes on the wall in letters of fire: "I am not your master but your obedient slave. You are my mistress" (our translation). Master and slave, tamer and beast — two versions of the same inequality.

For a couple it looks mundane. One decides what may be asked. The other silently gathers a "razor" — grievances, arguments, messages to be produced one day. Each is sure they are defending themselves from a beast, and each, in the other's eyes, slowly becomes one. Cupid puts it with bitter precision: he wounded himself with his own arrow and made Psyche his wife "so that, it seems, I should look like a beast to you, and you would cut off with a blade this head of mine, which carries these eyes that love you."

The tale knows another kind of strength too. When Psyche persuades her husband to let her sisters visit, she whispers endearments — "My honey, my husband, sweet soul of your Psyche!" — and "to the force and power of love's whisper the husband yielded against his will." In Apuleius, the god of love is overcome not by a razor but by a whisper.

The most precise advice about Strength comes from a reed by the river, when Venus sends Psyche for golden wool. Do not go near the sheep while the sun scorches them and "they are usually seized by a savage frenzy"; wait until "the frenzy of the sheep has died down" — and gather the wool "caught everywhere among the tangled branches". **Here the gold is not torn from a raging beast — it is picked up once the beast has calmed down.**

If strength in the couple has already become a threat and someone fears for their safety, this is not a matter for reading a tail. What is needed is real help: a local emergency number, a crisis line, a psychologist.

sections.h2: Atmosphere: Death at the centre, or a wedding in funeral dress
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya, the centre of a couple's chart is the atmosphere between the partners — what is inside and not on show. In couples with the 6-17-11 tail it is almost always 13, Death: in 98.8% of them. In the remaining 1.2% it is 22, The Fool. There are no other options.

This is no accident: here the centre is all but set by the tail itself. In a personal chart the entry of the tail is calculated as the sum of the karmic task and the centre. In a couple's chart it is not: each point is added up from the matching points of the two partners. But in the 6-17-11 tail the personal arithmetic works out by itself. The centre of such couples is always one of the two cards that, together with Strength, give The Lovers: 11 + 13 = 24, and 2 + 4 = 6; with the rare Fool, 11 + 22 = 33 → 6. And further: 6 + 11 = 17. If the numbers are read as a record, **Strength passed through Death gives The Lovers, and The Lovers together with Strength give The Star.** The couple's middle is calculated separately, from the middles of the two personal tails, and still matches the sum of the ends. This does not hold for every tail: in 50 of the 97 couple tails the middle and the sum of the ends differ.

Death in a couple's atmosphere is neither a threat nor a forecast. At its best, in Lisovskaya, it is a steady union with shared goals: the partner's past is accepted and left behind, changes in the partner are met calmly, and sometimes one helps the other leave a destructive relationship. At its worst it is a swing: so many changes that the other has nothing to lean on; one hurries the other to change; the features of an ex are glimpsed in the current partner; nitpicking over every trifle. Waite writes of the card's symbol as a passage "from lower to higher", Wen of the end of a stage and of how painful it is to part with the old.

Apuleius's tale is built exactly like this: each part of it dies so that the next can begin. The wedding is the funeral of a girl who was only a king's daughter. The night palace ends in lamplight. The wanderings end in sleep from a box. Psyche's mortal life ends with a cup of ambrosia. No stage is saved by being preserved — only by being allowed to end. For a couple with this tail this is perhaps the main secret of its atmosphere: the union holds not because nothing changes, but because the old is let go in time — first infatuation, old roles, the agreement "don't look".

sections.h2: The loop of the tail: the same mistake twice
paragraphs: When Lisovskaya analyses a couple's tail, she links the energies in pairs and all three together: each conclusion follows from its own combination. For 6-17-11 the links read like this.

ul: **The Lovers and The Star (6 + 17).** The wish for love meets the light. At best, a couple that is not afraid to see each other and becomes itself beside the other. At worst, love of the picture: a union that is shown first and lived afterwards.

**The Lovers and Strength (6 + 11).** The wish to be chosen meets power: who chose whom, who owes whom, who sets the terms. Hence jealousy and control — in Lisovskaya they grow from insecurity, not from strength.

**The Star and Strength (17 + 11).** Truth meets power. The same truth can be held up like a lamp, or like a razor. Constant criticism from The Star's downside and jibes from Strength's downside are one mistake: truth used as a weapon.

**All three (6 + 17 + 11).** Enchantment guarded by a prohibition breeds fear of what cannot be seen. Fear prepares a secret check. The check burns, and one of the two pulls away. Then comes the urge to bring the magic back — a little beauty from the box — and the couple falls into the same sleep again.

paragraphs: The tale says outright that the loop repeats. Waking Psyche, Cupid says: "Look, poor thing, you nearly perished again from the same curiosity." Psyche's two mistakes are really one: **she takes in secret what can only be received openly.** The first time, her husband's face; the second, beauty. The 6-17-11 tail does not condemn the wish to see — seeing is its very middle. It shows what becomes of a glance cast at night, in fear, with a razor in the other hand.

sections.h2: The way out: a marriage "not unequal"
paragraphs: The tale does not end with one side defeating the other. Jupiter gathers the gods and announces: "I will make this marriage not unequal, but lawful and in keeping with civil law." Psyche drinks ambrosia and becomes immortal — that is, her husband's equal. The unequal marriage of a mortal and a god is evened out not because someone won, but because both left their former positions: Cupid, the role of the invisible master of the night; Psyche, the role of the one who may not ask.

The strong version of the 6-17-11 tail is a couple that began as lovers in a dark palace and arrived at a union of two people who know each other in the light. **Strength in such couples is not the ability to endure or the ability to subdue, but the capacity to stay close to strong feelings, one's own and the other's, without turning them into either a weapon or a cage.**

ul: to say from the very start what one likes and what one doesn't, instead of guarding the enchantment with silence: Psyche was forbidden to ask — and she took up a razor;
to test doubts with a question asked with both present, not in secret and at night;
not to settle the big things at the peak: to wait until "the frenzy of the sheep has died down", and only then gather the gold;
to share power: no single partner controls the decisions, the money and the housework;
to hear the "sisters" — relatives, friends, other people's stories in the feed — as voices, not as a plan of action;
less shop window and fewer comparisons: a union does not have to look like a fairy tale to be one;
to let go of the union's former shapes once they have run their course, rather than mending them at any cost.

paragraphs: Eighteen centuries after Apuleius, C. S. Lewis retold this story from the point of view of Psyche's sister in his novel Till We Have Faces (1956). The narrator spends her life accusing the gods, and at the end understands why they are silent: "How can they meet us face to face till we have faces?" For a couple with the 6-17-11 tail this is perhaps the best formula for the main task. Love begins in the dark, with Cupid. Fullness begins when both have faces.

sections.h2: How the 6-17-11 tail comes about: an example with 14.08.1975 and 19.03.1979
paragraphs: Each point of a couple's chart is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, folded down to 22 by adding the digits. The couple's tail is not recalculated from its ends: entry is added to entry, middle to middle, task to task.

First partner, 14.08.1975. Day — 14, month — 8, year — 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Karmic task — 14 + 8 + 22 = 44 → 8. Centre — 14 + 8 + 22 + 8 = 52 → 7. Tail entry — 8 + 7 = 15, middle — 8 + 15 = 23 → 5. Personal tail — 15-5-8.

Second partner, 19.03.1979. Day — 19, month — 3, year — 1 + 9 + 7 + 9 = 26 → 8. Karmic task — 19 + 3 + 8 = 30 → 3. Centre — 19 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 33 → 6. Tail entry — 3 + 6 = 9, middle — 3 + 9 = 12. Personal tail — 9-12-3.
The couple's tail adds up like this:
Centre of the couple's chart — 7 + 6 = 13, Death. The couple's values — 12, The Hanged Man.

Neither of the two has The Lovers, The Star or Strength in their personal tail. The 6-17-11 tail is not one partner's inheritance; it is born only between them. This couple also has an echo of its own: The Lovers also stand on the point "Image of the couple" (14 + 19 = 33 → 6), and Strength on "What to create together" (8 + 3 = 11). This is a feature of these particular dates, not of every couple with this tail.

sections.h2: 6-17-11 in numbers: which couples it comes from
paragraphs: Going through every date since 1900 gives 97 different couple tails. 6-17-11 occurs in roughly one couple in 65 (1.545%) and ranks 23rd by frequency.

It is made up of just six combinations of personal tails. Most often it is 15-5-8 and 9-12-3, as in the example: that is 51% of such couples. Next come 18-9-9 and 6-8-20 (28%) and 15-8-11 and 9-9-18 (11%); the remaining three combinations make up 10% between them. In 61% of such couples, neither of the two personal tails contains any of the three cards. And nobody, ever, has The Star in their personal tail: the couple's middle, 17, is always made up of two other middles — 5 and 12, 9 and 8, 8 and 9, or 10 and 7. **This couple's Star belongs to the couple alone.**

The couple's values — the spiritual purpose, the path the two are to walk together — are one of three cards for such couples: 21, The World, in 39.5%; 12, The Hanged Man, in 34.5%; 3, The Empress, in 26%. This is a separate sphere of the reading, but the end of the tale, if you like, has all three. The feast of the gods, where the Muses sing and Venus herself dances, is The World, the circle completed. Psyche, hanging from the leg of her departing husband, "a hanging companion through the cloudy heights", and, in the underworld, refusing the soft seat and sitting down "humbly at the feet" of Proserpina, is The Hanged Man — the view from below and the refusal of the easy way. The daughter named Pleasure is The Empress. This is our reading, not a rule of the method.

ul: **Entry to the task — 6, The Lovers.** What the couple wants together: to be in love, to choose each other and to be chosen. Everything starts with this wish, and the same wish digs in its heels when the enchantment has to be tested by light.

**Middle of the task — 17, The Star.** How the couple travels its path: through openness and hope, through moments when the partner is seen whole, unveiled — and through the temptation to swap the truth for a pretty picture.

**Main task — 11, Strength.** What the couple has to learn: to deal with passion, anger, fear and power over each other with neither a knife nor a cage. Not to defeat the "beast" in the other, but to stop fearing it — and to make the union equal.

intro: A couple's tail does not predict events or pass sentence on a union. It is a pattern in which a couple recognises itself: where it is strong, where it stalls and what changes the script. What follows is an investigation: what the cards themselves say, what Arthur Edward Waite, Benebell Wen and Yuliana Lisovskaya, the author of the compatibility method, write about them, and what the numbers from the site's engine show.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 6-17-11 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task, written in three points of the compatibility chart: entry to the task — The Lovers, middle — The Star, main task — Strength. The couple begins with the wish for love and enchantment, travels through openness and moments when everything is seen without embellishment, and has one main thing to learn — to handle passion, anger, fear and power over each other without suppression and without a cage, so that the union becomes equal.

faq.q: Is this the same as the personal karmic tail 6-17-11?
faq.a: No. The same three numbers also occur as a personal tail — for 2,052 birth dates since 1900 — but it is a different calculation, and the points have different roles. A personal tail is calculated from one date; a couple's tail is the sum of the points of two charts and is read as a task for two. Personal readings do not carry over to the couple; the personal tail has its own article on the site.

faq.q: Can a couple's tail have the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails produced by all dates since 1900, the numbers 6, 17 and 11 occur only in this order. The same set in another sequence does not come up for a couple.

faq.q: Is Death at the centre of the chart a bad sign for such a couple?
faq.a: No. The centre of a couple's chart is the atmosphere between the partners, and 13 there speaks of a union that goes through change and renewal, not of a threat. In couples with the 6-17-11 tail, Death stands at the centre in 98.8% of cases: it follows from the numbers themselves. The difficulty of this atmosphere is the swings and the attempts to remake the partner; its strength is the ability to let go of what has run its course, in time.

faq.q: Is the 6-17-11 tail a sentence or a prediction?
faq.a: Neither. The tail does not predict events, dates or break-ups, and does not say whether a couple suits each other. It shows where the couple stumbles and what it can learn together. As in Apuleius's tale, the main work is not to overcome the other but to see them in the light.

faq.q: Do the partners need The Lovers, The Star or Strength in their personal charts?
faq.a: No. In 61% of such couples neither of the two personal tails contains any of these cards, and neither partner ever has The Star in their personal tail. A couple's tail is born from the sum of two charts, so its theme may be new to both.

report.h3: Gold is gathered once the beast has calmed

report: The tale knows another kind of strength. In Apuleius, the god of love is overcome not by a razor but by a whisper: "to the force and power of love's whisper the husband yielded against his will." And the most precise advice about Strength comes from a reed by the river: do not go near the sheep while "they are usually seized by a savage frenzy", wait until "the frenzy of the sheep has died down", and gather the golden wool from the branches. **The gold is not torn from a raging beast — it is picked up once the beast has calmed down.**

Hence the practice: to say from the very start what one likes and what one doesn't, instead of guarding the enchantment with silence; to test doubts with a question asked with both present, not in secret and at night; not to settle the big things at the peak; to share power, so that no single partner controls the decisions, the money and the housework; to let go of the union's former shapes once they have run their course. If strength in the couple has already become a threat and someone fears for their safety, this is not a matter for reading a tail: real help is needed — a local emergency number or crisis line, a psychologist.

The tale does not end with one side defeating the other. Jupiter promises: "I will make this marriage not unequal," and Psyche becomes immortal, her husband's equal. The strong version of the 6-17-11 tail is a couple that began as lovers in a dark palace and arrived at **a union of two people who know each other in the light**. C. S. Lewis, who retold this story eighteen centuries later, found a formula for it: "How can they meet us face to face till we have faces?" Love begins in the dark. Fullness comes when both have faces.

unit.title: A lamp instead of a razor

captions.M: To want love and enchantment, as at the very start
captions.N: To see each other in the light, not a pretty picture
captions.D: To make the union equal: no master and no slave

unit.meaning: Your task is to make the union equal: ask openly rather than check in secret, and don't leave power in one pair of hands.
